en: Preface to the Commentary on the Vow for Rebirth in the Western Paradise:
Someone once asked me, "Among the texts concerning the Pure Land found in various sutras, there are generally three versions.
Their phrasing and meaning are all worthy of veneration; yet you alone praise the one composed by Master Yunqi with such fervor. Furthermore, as for its text..."
The meaning is not difficult to understand; Yunqi’s brief commentary already makes it clear. Why, then, did the Master further provide an annotated explanation? I replied:
"Although other texts may be worthy of veneration, their phrasing and meaning are not exhaustive. This alone is the text of the vow."
The meaning is comprehensive and the phrasing is complete; please explain this further. This text of vows consists of six major sections:
first, the arousal of the bodhicitta; second, the repentance of the three obstacles; third, the establishment of the four great vows; and fourth, the aspiration to be reborn in the Pure Land.
The fifth is returning to enter the Sahā world; the sixth is the general dedication of merit. These six chapters provide a complete account from beginning to end. Why is this?

For in the Dharma-gate of Buddha-remembrance, Bodhicitta is the most essential. If the great resolve is not awakened, the Pure Land is difficult to attain. Therefore, it begins with the awakening of Bodhicitta.
Yet, though the aspiration is established, one is still entangled by afflictions and karma. Once the retribution of past deeds returns, how [can one remain steadfast]?

Thus one attains liberation; therefore, this is followed by the repentance for the three obstacles (*tri-āvaraṇa*). Once afflictions and delusions are purified and the burden of karmic retribution is entirely removed, yet if the great vows are not firm, one may easily regress from practice;
therefore, this is extended by means of the four great vows (*catur-mahāpraṇidhāna*).

When the aspiration of the mind and the vows arise together, delusions and karma are both extinguished, whereby *samādhi* can be accomplished and rebirth in the nine lotuses becomes easy; therefore, this is concluded with the essential practice of seeking birth in the Pure Land.
To aspire solely for one’s own benefit is called the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna); to universally vow to benefit others is alone termed being a Great Being (Mahāsattva).

Therefore, following this, one returns to enter the Sahā world. Since both self and others, as well as cause and effect, and phenomenon and principle are all perfected, the text concludes with a general dedication of merit.
These six methods are such that not one may be omitted. If one is missing, one will obtain only the minor fruits of humans and devas.
If two are missing, one will receive the evil retributions of the three miserable realms. If three are missing, indolence easily arises. If four are missing, it is difficult to escape saṃsāra.

If five are missing, one becomes a solitary śrāvaka. If all six are missing, the law of cause and effect is not perfected. Regarding other texts on the Pure Land, they merely speak of seeking rebirth there.

Regarding this vow, there is no text concerning its integration [into practice]. Since the initial arousal of the mind and the establishment of the oath have not been clearly elucidated, and the confession and dedication have likewise not been set forth, the phrasing and meaning are therefore incomplete.
Although Yunqi did provide a commentary on this vow text, he merely explained the general intent;
as for its underlying principles and logic, they remain latent and undeveloped, making it difficult even for those with dull faculties at the beginning of their path to comprehend.
I have provided this exegesis because I do not shrink from elaborate detail. For this Dharma-gate belongs to the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao);

if one does not clarify the Perfect Principle, how can one be a person of the Perfect [Teaching]? If one is not a person of the Perfect [Teaching], how could they give rise to a Perfect Vow? How could they cultivate Perfect Practice?

Therefore, in these annotations, when the Four Great Vows are mentioned, they necessarily lead back to the Unconditioned (wu zuo); when dedication (huixiang) is mentioned, it is invariably [directed toward] the Unconditioned.
It possesses these three qualities: there is no phenomenon that is not identical with principle, and every aspiration accords with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*).

Furthermore, fearing that practitioners in the末法 (final age) may have little familiarity with the meanings of the teachings, I have not dared to describe all the names and characteristics in detail; rather, I have captured their essential meaning and transformed the phrasing.
This is intended only for beginners; how could it possibly be heard by those of long-standing study?
Yet, there are those who, through these few words, gain a slight understanding of even a fragment of its meaning, and subsequently seek out the Mahāyāna sūtras and the writings of the patriarchs.

Only then do they realize that the dharma-gates of bodhisattva practice and the causes and conditions of the Buddhas' attainment of enlightenment are entirely contained herein. Furthermore, how could there be any other dharma existing outside of this *praṇidhāna* text?
"Truly so! This is the reason why I have praised and provided this commentary. The questioner responded with respectful assent and withdrew.
I, therefore, followed the preceding arguments to compose this preface.
Written by the śrāmaṇera Shi-xian of Yushan in Eastern Wu, on the full moon of the twelfth month in the year of Bingwu, the fourth year of the Yongzheng era,
at Haiyun Jingshe in Jiaomen, Hainan. Annotated Exposition of the *Aspiration for Rebirth in the Western Pure Land*.
Composed by the Great Master Lianchi of Yunqi;
annotated by the junior disciple śrāmaṇera Shixian for the sake of later students.
*Text on Making Vows for Rebirth in the Western Paradise*
This commentary on the text of the vow is divided into two main sections: first, the title; second, the entry into the text.
Regarding the five characters of the title, there are both general and specific meanings. "Western" (*xīfāng*) is the specific name, while the character "vow" (*wén*) is the general name.
Within the specific name, the two characters "Western" refer to that which is vowed, and the character "vow" refers to the act of making the vow. The character "to make" (*fā*) possesses—
This encompasses both the object and the subject. Furthermore, the Western Land is the place toward which one aspires, while aspiration is the mind that initiates the resolve.
To speak of the West includes both the primary and secondary retributions (*āśraya-vipāka* and *upabhoga-vipāka*); to speak of making a vow subsumes both self-benefit and the benefit of others.

The secondary retribution consists of the adornments of the seven treasures, wherein the four lands are perfectly interfused; the primary retribution consists of Amitābha and his holy assembly, who are the three bodies in one essence.
Regarding the four lands: first, the Land of Constant Quiescent Light; second, the Land of True Reward Adornment; third, the Land of Expedient Means with Remainder;
and fourth, the Land of Common Dwelling for Ordinary Beings and Sages. Regarding the three bodies: the Dharma-body, the Reward-body, and the Response-body.

There should be distinctions of superiority and inferiority among these: the superior is majestic and sublime, while the inferior is sixteen or eight feet in height. Question: Since there is only one Western [Pure Land], why...
Question: If there are four lands, and yet it is but a single Buddha, how can there be three bodies? Is this not a case of fragmentation and division? Answer:
It is like a single moon that appears with different reflections and shadows; or like a single mirror that reflects various images and glows with different lights.
Has the moon ever been fragmented, or have the reflections ever been divided from the mirror? Such is the Dharma.

The body is like the moon; the reward body (saṃbhogakāya) is like its light; the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) is like its reflection. The land of serene light (śāntaprabhāsa-kṣetra) is like the substance of the mirror; the land of true reward (samyakphala-kṣetra) is like the light of the mirror;

the land of skillful means and common residence (upāyasahabhuva-kṣetra) is like the images reflected in the mirror. In the Buddha, there is only the single Dharma-nature body (dharmatākāya) and the land of serene light;
yet for the sake of sentient beings, he manifests two bodies corresponding to the three lower lands for those on the ten stages and the three [categories of] sages.

The Mind-Bodhisattva (the thirty minds consisting of the ten abodes, ten practices, and ten transferences) manifests as the Perfect Reward Body, dwelling in the Land of True Reward, appearing in both superior and inferior forms for the sake of Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas.
Dwelling in the Land of Expedient Means, he appears in both superior and inferior forms for the sake of ordinary beings and Bodhisattvas who have first resolved their minds.

Dwelling in the Land of Common Residence, he manifests as the Inferior Response Body. (In this context, the bodies and lands that accord with the capacities of beings are discussed only from the general perspective of the Complete Teaching; if one were to explain them fully, there are four [lands]).

The teachings regarding their characteristics differ in a thousand ways; fearing prolixity, I shall not cite them here). Question: Are these four lands situated in the same location, or are they distinct from one another? Answer:
They are both the same and different. They are the same in that they are like a single body of water, yet there are four distinct perceptions of it by devas, humans, fish, and ghosts.

They are different in that their respective domains and locations are not the same; however, those above can know those below, while those below cannot know those above. It is the same with the lands of responsive transformation (nirmāṇa):

Bodhisattvas can respond by dwelling together through skillful means, and Śrāvakas can also respond by dwelling together, whereas ordinary beings merely dwell in the land of common residence (sahabhū) and cannot reach the higher realms; thus it is said, "it is likewise. [This refers to] Amitābha.

The ultimate [realization] is the three bodies (trikāya). The noble assembly partially attains the three bodies, whereas ordinary beings possess only the principle-endowment (*rigpa*) and lack the phenomenal function.

These bodies and lands differ only according to the distinctions in the perceptions of sentient beings; in reality, however, the environment and its inhabitants are non-dual, and essence and function are without difference.
Therefore, it is said that they are a single, perfectly interfused entity. As for self-benefit, one manifests in this life to sever...
Delusion. Rebirth in a future life for the benefit of others is likewise so. Furthermore, the term "to arouse" (fa) means to incite;
the term "vow" (yuan) means to aspire. Incitement is like an arrow leaving the bowstring—its momentum does not cease.
Aspiration is like longing for a beautiful form or scheming for great profit; thus one first arouses the vow to be reborn there, and after a short while...

Those who are indolent and lazy do not possess the "aspiration" (*praṇidhāna*). Furthermore, those who speak of the Pure Land with their mouths while their hearts long for this Sahā world do not possess the "vow" (*praṇidhāna*) either.

Moreover, the single word "vow" encompasses both faith and practice. As for faith: it holds that the causes and effects of oneself and others are not in vain, and that both principle and phenomena are not empty.

(To believe that one's own mind is the Buddha, and that others are likewise so; that reciting the Buddha’s name is the cause, and attaining Buddhahood through rebirth is the fruit; that the Western Land is the phenomenon, and the nature of the mind apart from it is the principle.)
Because each and every [aspect] is true, it is said to be "not false. As for practice (*caryā*), one should focus exclusively on holding the Name, without distraction or dissipation.
As for the vow (*praṇidhāna*), one should delight in it heart and mind, aspiring toward it in every thought-moment. These three matters—faith, practice, and the vow—are such that none may be missing.

There may be those who possess faith and practice but lack the vow; however, there has never been anyone who possesses the vow but lacks faith and practice. Question: Someone hears it said regarding the West...
Question: If one develops a heart of joyful aspiration for the Pure Land but does not practice mindfulness of the Buddha, will one attain rebirth there?

Answer: If one truly develops a heart of joyful aspiration, one will certainly give rise to a longing [for rebirth]. If one gives rise to such longing, one will necessarily practice mindfulness of the Buddha. If one has joyful aspiration but lacks longing, it is certainly not true joyful aspiration.
If one has longing but does not practice mindfulness of the Buddha, how can that be considered longing? True joyful aspiration and longing consist in the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha.

There has never been a Buddha who did not attain rebirth [in the Pure Land]. Question: Suppose there is a person here who likewise desires, seeks, and contemplates [rebirth], yet their worldly mind is heavy and they are greedily attached to the dust and toil of the world;
will such a person attain rebirth? Answer: It depends solely on whether one’s resolve is fierce and one does not fear the strength of the thief.
If one’s heart of aspiration is truly earnest and one’s focused mindfulness is single-minded, then even though their attachment may be strong...
If the heavy burden gradually becomes light, one shall likewise attain rebirth in the Pure Land. It would be like discarding silver to take gold, or casting away fish to take the bear’s paw;
what difficulty could there be? However, I fear that the power of one's vows may not overcome the power of attachment, and the mindfulness of the Buddha may not surpass the cravings of desire.
If one remains indolent and distracted, half-believing and half-doubting, then I can do nothing for such a person.

[He] asked again: "If performing good leads to birth in heaven and committing evil leads to entry into hell, and these occur naturally without one having to make a formal vow, then the same should apply to rebirth through mindfulness of the Buddha (*nianfo*).
Why must one wait for a vow before being born [there]? The answer was: "The causes and effects within the three realms are induced by karma;
they certainly do not depend on a vow to come into being. However, seeking birth in the Western Land is the supreme, world-transcending correct cause. If one lacks..."
Regarding the solemn commitment of the great vow: even if one recites the Buddha’s name, success will certainly not be achieved.
It is like an ox walking a familiar path; although there is no driver, it knows where to go home. But if it walks an unfamiliar path, it will certainly have no direction;
it must have a driver holding the end of the rope and further applying the whip, only then will it proceed. The nature of sentient beings is like that ox. Part Three.
The realms are like a well-trodden path; the Western Quarter is like a path yet to be traveled. Aspiration is like a charioteer; faith is like the hands;

mindfulness is like the end of a rope; and the vow is like a whip. Rebirth [in the Pure Land] is like walking along a road. Without aspiration, one will not be reborn, just as an ox without a driver cannot go.

Therefore, it is essential to give rise to aspiration. Question: Regarding the three—faith, practice, and aspiration—I have already received your instructions. However, throughout the ten directions...
"All lands have Buddha-fields; why then must one specifically aspire only for the West? Answer:
"In that land, Amitābha Buddha has a profound karmic affinity with the sentient beings of this land, whereas other Buddhas do not. For this reason, one seeks that realm exclusively."

One does not wish for other directions. Furthermore, within that land, the environment and the inhabitants (the *niśraya-vipāka* and *sambhoga-vipāka*) surpass those of the ten directions and are praised by all Buddhas.
It is not only ordinary beings who wish to go there; Bodhisattvas do so as well. It is not only this direction that they wish to go; it is the same for all other directions.

Since the eight difficulties and the three miserable realms are absent, and the three poisons and the eight sufferings likewise do not exist, clothing and food appear spontaneously, and [the lifespan is]...
The lifespan is immeasurable. Water birds and forest trees are all able to preach the Dharma. The number of śrāvakas and mahāsattvas is exceedingly great;
these most excellent beings assemble together in one place. For this reason, in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*, Śākyamuni Tathāgata exhorted us with earnest and repeated instruction:
"You sentient beings should make a vow to be reborn in that land. Again, he asked about the Patriarchs.

The Master said: "The wise know that the mind is Buddha; the ignorant delight in going to the Western Land. Speaking from this perspective, the ignorant should simply recite the Buddha's name, while the wise ought indeed to practice Chan.
If one were to universally exhort [everyone] toward rebirth there, I fear it would contravene the intent of the Patriarchs;

such a view is not a comprehensive discourse. [The interlocutor] replied: "If you say that rebirth is for the ignorant, then how do you account for the various Patriarchs of the past who [attained rebirth in] the Lotus..."
The eminent worthies of our school, even down to Aśvaghoṣa, Nāgārjuna, Mañjuśrī, and Samantabhadra, were all likewise deluded and ignorant of the mind.
One should know that speaking according to the ultimate principle, only the Buddha alone is called the Wise One; all others are deluded.
If one were to discuss this from the perspective of phenomena, there would be a thousand differences—how could it be easily explained? Alas! The Patriarch shattered [all attachments].
People cling to existence, and thus they utter such words. Now you cling to emptiness; you have contracted an illness from the medicine.
You do not realize that while an illness of existence is easy to dispel, an illness of emptiness is difficult to eliminate. Who in the world could be more utterly foolish than you? He asked again:

"In antiquity, there were those who made a vow to be reborn in a future life in a central land, where they would grow up to meet an enlightened teacher, leave the household life with right faith, and enter the Way in their youth."

As for this, what does it mean? The answer is: In the past, when the Semblance Dharma (Pratirūpaka-yuga) was flourishing, the faculties of sentient beings were still sharp, enlightened teachers were easy to find, and entering the Path was not difficult.
Even if one did not attain clarity in the present life, it could be expected in a future birth; thus, this vow was made.
Now it is not so. The Buddha-Dharma declines ever further; the faculties of men grow ever duller. The heterodox abound while the orthodox are few;

retreat is easy, but progress is difficult. Inner obstructions and external demons—there is no one who does not possess them. Enlightened teachers and virtuous friends are rare in this world and difficult to encounter.

We see only those who have left the household life filling the earth, yet we have never heard of anyone who has attained the Way. If one has failed for successive kalpas, how can one succeed in a future life? Alas!
The errors of the former masters are clearly evident. The *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* provides a prophetic record that serves as authentic testimony [stating]:

"In the final five hundred years, though billions upon billions of people practice, not a single one will attain the Way; only by relying on the Dharma-gate of mindfulness of the Buddha can one transcend birth and death. Yet there are those who, ignorant of what is beneficial or harmful, recklessly imitate the ancients and still make such vows;
this is a mistake. Furthermore, when speaking of the Middle Kingdom, how could it compare to the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*An-yang*)? When speaking of...
Regarding enlightened teachers, who could surpass Amitābha? Regarding leaving the household life, who could equal the horizontal transcendence of the three realms?
Regarding entering the Way, who could equal the seeing of the Buddha upon the blossoming of the flower and the realization of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*)?

To not aspire for such things and instead aspire for the Sahā world—I believe such a person is truly deluded and stubborn. Question: Seeking rebirth in the Western Land is indeed my aspiration; however...

Question: "I am a lowly ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*). My sinful karma is deep and heavy, while my merit and virtue are slight. How can I easily attain birth in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*Sukhāvatī*)? Answer:

"In other gateways for studying the Path, one must rely on the practitioner’s own power (*svabala*). Birth through mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*) relies entirely upon the power of Amitābha’s vows (*praṇidhānabala*).

Because one's own power is difficult to achieve, it has not been accomplished throughout successive kalpas. Because the power of others is easy to rely upon, [birth] can be achieved in a single lifetime."
Therefore, one may attain rebirth in a single day or seven days; even with ten recitations or a single thought, one can behold the Buddha.
Even for those who have committed the ten grave evils, the Buddha does not abandon them—how much more so for ordinary people who practice the ten virtues?

If one makes a vow in this life to recite the Buddha’s name, how could they fail to attain rebirth? Furthermore, a single invocation of His Great Name extinguishes the sins of eighty billion kalpas; how much more so [for repeated recitation]? How could it be otherwise?
Doubt that one's karma is heavy. To hold the holy name for even a moment is superior to practicing generosity for a hundred years; why worry that one’s merit is slight?

Simply cultivate faith, and you will certainly not be deceived. He asked again: "The Inner Court of Tuṣita is near to this world, and there are Bodhisattvas in the stage of succession who preach the Dharma therein.
One could also ascend there to draw near to these Great Beings. Why must one transcend [this realm]?"
This land far surpasses other realms. Answer: The Pure Land of the West relies upon the power of Amitābha’s vows to welcome and lead beings there to rebirth;
therefore, although it is distant, it is easy to reach. The Inner Court of Tuṣita requires the practitioner’s power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) to ascend;
therefore, although it is near, it is difficult to be born there. If one lacks meditative concentration, it is like wishing to fly without wings. To seek [rebirth]...
Having ascended, one may fall back down. Furthermore, regarding the pleasures of that celestial realm, even those with a beginner’s mind are still deluded.

The three men from the Western Regions serve as a solemn warning (*yinpian*). As the *Xiyuji* states: "Asanga, Vasubandhu, and Simhabuddhi—the third being the elder brother—made a vow to be reborn together in Tuṣita to see Maitreya Buddha. They agreed that whoever should first ascend to be born there must return to inform the others.

Later, Simhabuddhi passed away first, yet no news was heard for a long time. Vasubandhu followed him in death, and another year passed before a message finally arrived. Asanga asked, 'Have you been born in Tuṣita? He replied, 'I have already been born; I have seen Maitreya face-to-face. Moreover...

He asked, "Where is Siṃhabuddhi? He replied, "He was born in the outer courtyard; being attached to sensual pleasures, he does not see the Bodhisattva. For this reason, he has not come. By reporting these signs, it is known that even a minor bodhisattva is like this—how much more so an ordinary person? How could one not know what is beneficial and what is harmful?
He asked again, "The adornments of the environment and inhabitants of the Eastern Medicine Buddha’s land are no different from those of the Western [Pure Land]."

Furthermore, there are eight great bodhisattvas who manifest the path at the time of death, through which one may also attain rebirth [in the Pure Land]. Why, then, must one specifically vow for the Western Pure Land?
Answer: The *Bhaiṣajyaguru Sūtra* primarily focuses on the elimination of calamities and the extension of life; it does not exclusively exhort rebirth [in the Pure Land].

The statement that "the Bodhisattvas show the way" refers to a specific class of beings with indeterminate roots of goodness who wish to be reborn in various directions to make offerings to Buddhas and hear the Dharma.
Such individuals possess both merit and wisdom; thus, all their aspirations are fulfilled.

Consequently, upon hearing the name of Bhaisajyaguru Buddha, they are reborn in his land as soon as they bring him to mind. The eight great Bodhisattvas specifically show them the way and point it out.
They merely return to their own places; it is not necessarily the case that they are reborn in that land. Therefore, it is said:
"Some may, because of this, be born in the heavens or among humans, becoming wheel-turning kings who govern the four continents and establish the four classes of people in the ten wholesome deeds.
Is this not possible only for those who possess both merit and wisdom? Now, in the land of Amitābha Buddha, there is an exclusive exhortation.

Rebirth is extensively discussed in the various sutras; one shall go to the ten directions, where the holy assembly of Amitābha extends a hand to receive and lead one forth, and the Buddhas such as Śākyamuni praise and protect one with mindfulness.
Yet, you abandon the universal path to travel a narrow road, clinging to temporary words while discarding the eternal discourse.
Since there is no fixed direction toward either the east or the west, and since your recitation is likewise inconsistent, you possess no merit.
Furthermore, those with little supernormal power who have not yet attained birth according to their aspirations end up wandering aimlessly; can this not be considered a matter for careful scrutiny?
Now, wishing to unify one's resolve and concentrate one's direction—if one does not return to the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang), where else will one go?

Because one concentrates one's direction, it is called "the West. Because one unifies one's resolve, it is called "making a vow" (*praṇidhāna*). As for "text" (*vyañjana*), it refers to the words and phrases that serve as the means of expression.

Furthermore, there are general and specific aspects to vows (*praṇidhāna*). Generally, they refer to the Four Great Vows (*caturmahāpraṇidhāna*); specifically, they refer to the various vows issued according to one's own mind.

Moreover, generally, all are termed "vows"; specifically, "bodhicitta" is termed the "arising of the mind," the Four Great Vows are termed the "arising of the resolve," and seeking rebirth in the Western Land is termed the "arising of a vow.
Furthermore, dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) is also termed a "vow," as in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
In the text of the Ten Dedications of Vajra, each and every one states, "May all sentient beings [attain suchness]," and so forth.

Furthermore, the aspiration to be reborn in the Western Pure Land subsumes all vows for bodhi, as well as all the Buddha-dharmas of the ten directions and the three periods of time, without exception.
Therefore, this title is placed at the beginning of the work. Moreover, the matters and principles of this vow-text are complete.

The preparations are complete. The practices and vows are profound and vast. All who possess wisdom should savor these words and diligently practice these deeds, so that both self and others may benefit and both cause and effect may be fulfilled;
let it not be merely a matter of written characters, spoken language, or the chanting of sounds in harmony.
The initial explanation of the title is concluded. Part Two: Entering the Text, which is divided into two sections. First, taking refuge and requesting empowerment. Second...
The Vow of Dedication. First:
I bow my head to the Great Teacher who guides sentient beings, To the Western Land of Peace and Bliss.
Now I make this vow to be reborn there; May you, in your compassion, graciously accept me.
The first two lines of the verse constitute the taking of refuge; the latter two lines constitute the request for empowerment.
At the beginning of making a vow, one must first take refuge in the Buddha in order to seek realization of this mind. "Prostrating" (*kai-shou*) refers to the ritual of paying homage to the Buddha;
it means to place one’s head upon the ground, remain there for a brief moment, and then rise—hence it is called "prostrating"—and it expresses reverence.
This is the ultimate [state]. The Land of Peace and Bliss in the West is the Great Teacher who, through his *pariṇāmanā-vipāka* (retributive environment), guides sentient beings;

it is the *sambhogakāya* (the body of recompense). Regarding the term "Land of Peace and Bliss": it is called "Peace" because it is free from the eight sufferings, and it is called "Bliss" because it is free from the three poisons.
That which is governed by the Dharma King is called a kingdom. As for "guiding and leading": sentient beings are submerged in the ocean of suffering;
the Buddha receives them with the hand of wisdom and causes them to emerge. Attached to the five desires, the Buddha entices them with various forms of happiness and causes them to leave them behind;
hence it is called "guiding and leading. As for "the Guide": he leads people by means of the right path. Sentient beings are deluded and inverted.
They take suffering to be pleasure and the perverse to be correct, remaining ignorant of the essential means of liberation.

The Buddha distinguishes for them that this Sahā world is suffering while the Western Land is bliss, causing them to give rise to longing for the latter and revulsion toward the former, so that they may form the aspiration to be reborn there; therefore, he is called a "Guide.

Non-Buddhists do not know the distinction between the perverse and the correct, falsely establishing their own sects; such teachers are not guides. Śrāvakas are able to escape the three realms, yet...
To transform sentient beings: this is being a guide, not merely a teacher. Although a bodhisattva can transform sentient beings, though they are a guide, they are not called "Great.
Only the World-Honored One Amitābha, riding the ship of great vows, enters the sea of birth and death;
he does not cling to this shore, does not dwell on the other shore, and does not remain in midstream, yet he guides sentient beings to reach the other shore. It is thus.
Benefiting all beings throughout the ten directions and across the three periods of time without a moment’s rest, you alone are called the Great Teacher.
That I now wish to go [to you] is merely my own delusion; I pray only that you will take me under your care. This is a request for your protection.
"Loving-kindness" (maitrī) means cherishing; "compassion" (karuṇā) means pitying. Like a mother thinking of her child, may your heart never abandon me.

This is called "embracing" (*parigraha*). The first section, "Taking Refuge and Requesting Empowerment," is concluded. △ Second, "Making Vows and Dedication" has two parts: first, making vows; second, dedication.
The first part [making vows] further has two sections: first, self-benefit; second, benefiting others. The first [self-benefit] further has three sections:
first, generating the mind and upholding the name; second, repenting the three obstructions; third, making vows. Now, the first [generating the mind and upholding the name]:
I, the disciple [Name], for the sake of the four debts of gratitude, the three realms of existence, and all sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm,

seek the unsurpassed Bodhi-path of the One Vehicle of all Buddhas; therefore, with single-minded devotion, I shall hold in mind the vast name of Amitābha Buddha, endowed with ten thousand virtues, aspiring to be born in the Pure Land.
"Universally for the four debts of gratitude and so forth" refers to the objects of focus. "Seeking all Buddhas and so forth" refers to the mind that gives rise to aspiration.
"Single-mindedly upholding the recitation and so forth" refers to the Buddhas who are to be recollected. "Aiming for rebirth in the Pure Land" refers to the place one hopes to reach.
Indeed, when giving rise to the bodhicitta, one must first take an object as a condition; if this object were absent, the mind would have nothing upon which to rely.

The "recompense based upon" (依報) encompasses the "primary retribution" (正報). "Sentient beings of the Dharma-realm" refers to all sentient beings throughout the infinite worlds of the ten directions;
it also refers to the sentient beings of the nine realms. Because they are neither two nor three, they are called "one.
Because they are conveyed, they are called a "vehicle" (乘). "Unsurpassed" means there is nothing above it. "Bodhi" is the wisdom capable of awakening. It is said:
Not only is it for one's own benefit alone, but one desires to universally serve the four debts of gratitude;

nor is it merely for the sake of those four debts, but also to universally deliver all beings of the six realms and four modes of birth. Furthermore, it is not for the sake of a single set of three realms, six paths, or four births, but rather for the sake of all sentient beings throughout the infinite worlds of the ten directions, desiring to bring them across and liberate them so that they may...
All shall attain the path of the supreme Bodhi of the One Vehicle; it is for this reason that they give rise to this mind. "Single-mindedly" means not being distracted by other matters.
"Maintaining mindfulness" means receiving [the name] and not forgetting it. It is a single name that possesses ten thousand virtues;

thus it is called the "Great Name of Ten Thousand Virtues. "Expectation" (ki) means hope. Because it is free from the five turbidities, it is named the Pure Land. Thus, one recites the Buddha's name...
If one does not give rise to the great bodhicitta, one will never attain rebirth, even if one accords with the original vows of Amitābha.
Furthermore, though one may give rise to bodhicitta, if one does not single-mindedly practice the recitation of the Buddha's name, one will likewise not attain rebirth.

Therefore, one must take the arousal of bodhicitta as the direct cause and the recitation of the Buddha's name as the auxiliary condition before one can expect to be born in the Pure Land. This is the practice for those who cultivate the path of purity.
One may not know this. △ Second, repentance for the three obstructions.
Furthermore, because karma is heavy and merit is light, obstructions are deep and wisdom is shallow; the defiled mind easily flares up, while pure virtue is difficult to accomplish.
Now, before the Buddha, we lift our five limbs with diligence and lay bare our single mind to repent with utmost sincerity. Myself and all sentient beings, throughout kalpas of time...

Up until now, I have been deluded regarding my fundamentally pure mind, giving rein to greed, anger, and ignorance, thereby defiling the three karmas with immeasurable and boundless sinful stains and immeasurable and boundless karmic debts of enmity; may they all be completely extinguished.
Furthermore, the following clarifies the causes for repentance; now, the subsequent section clarifies the method of repentance.
"I and all sentient beings" correctly sets forth the confession. This passage follows from the preceding text:

although one recites the Buddha's name, arouses the aspiration, and hopes to be born in the Pure Land, my karmic offenses are heavy and thick, while my merit and goodness are slight; thus, the conditions of obstruction are profound.
My wisdom is shallow and my mind-consciousness is defiled, burning like a blazing fire; I have achieved not a single pure merit.
To speak of this, how could one not feel sorrow? Indeed, ordinary people in the final age are as dull-witted as this.
Such karmic obstructions can hinder a practitioner from attaining rebirth in the Pure Land—what is to be done? This is the repentance.

This is a matter of urgent priority. Regarding the statement that "karma is heavy while merit is light": karma refers to the ten non-virtues (*daśākuśala*), and merit refers to the ten virtues (*daśakuśala*).
As for the ten non-virtues: there are three of the body—namely, killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct; four of speech—namely, false speech, frivolous speech, divisive speech, and harsh speech;
and three of the mind—namely, greed, hatred, and delusion. To reverse these ten non-virtues is what is called the ten virtues. Thus it is said.
If the gravity is heavy, one fully commits the ten evil deeds; if the gravity is light, one practices a single good deed alone.

Furthermore, the ten evil deeds of the superior grade are called heavy karma, while the ten good deeds of the inferior grade are called light merit (as with the evil karma of killing: taking the parents, teachers, or monks as the superior grade, other humans as the middle grade, and animals or minute insects as the inferior grade;

all others may be understood by analogy. The ten good deeds are the reverse of this, which can be grasped through reflection). Moreover, performing evil with fervent intensity is called heavy karma; whereas [performing it] casually...

However, practicing goodness is called "light merit. Yet, if one harbors anger toward others, cursing them to perish quickly, or striking them with a staff so that they immediately die, this karma is heavy.
Furthermore, if one has only just begun to recite the Buddha’s name and immediately complains of mouth-sourness, or wishes to prostrate and again says there is pain in the waist—this is light merit.
Regarding the statement that "obstructions are deep and wisdom is shallow," there are two kinds of obstructions.
There are two kinds of obstacles: first, external obstacles; second, internal obstacles. External obstacles are of two types: first, the pressure of worldly conditions (*rajas-pratyaya*);
second, the entanglements of Māras and non-Buddhists. Internal obstacles are likewise of two types: first, illness and untimely death;

second, ignorance and inverted views. Wisdom is of two types: first, the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-prajñā*); second, the wisdom of ultimate reality (*tattva-prajñā*). [This is attained through] hearing and reflection.

Cultivation serves as the expedient means, while the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*) constitutes the reality. There are two types of the Path of Vision: first, that of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*); second, that of the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*).
Within the vision of the Great Vehicle, there are further two kinds: first, emptiness and the provisional; second, the Middle Way (*madhyamā pratipad*). The Middle Way is again twofold:
first, the "mere middle" (*butong zhongdao*); second, the "perfect middle" (*yuanzhong*). If one discusses the depth and shallowness according to these various wisdoms:

Wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) is shallow; wisdom derived from reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) is deep. Even within the Middle Way, that which is merely provisional is shallow, while the perfect Middle Way (*pariniṣpanna-madhyama*) is deep.

This can be understood by comparing these points against one another. When it is said that the obstacles are deep, it means that internal and external factors attack simultaneously. When it is said that wisdom is shallow, it means that the cultivation through hearing is thin and one's understanding is meager.

Consequently, there are those who, as soon as they wish to practice, immediately develop malignant diseases; or those who, just as they are able to turn toward the Path, encounter heterodox influences.

The Master said: "This obstacle is profound. Furthermore, there are those who, having not yet attained the stage of an inner ordinary person (ābhyantarapṛthagjana), claim they have already transcended the Buddha-ground;

or those with a slight proficiency in worldly knowledge declare themselves to have entered the gate of enlightenment. This is because their wisdom is shallow. Greed, anger, and delusion are called defiled minds, while precepts, concentration, and wisdom are called pure virtues.
Regarding the statement that [anger] is easily inflamed: anger is like a flame; when it encounters dry grass, it spreads and intensifies."
Their height increases. Craving is like a lotus fiber; though cut by a dull blade, it remains connected and continuous.

Ignorance weaves a dense net of views; the more one is bound, the more one is entangled. The roots of the perverse are planted deeply, flourishing and expanding ever further. Regarding that which is difficult to accomplish:

as for precepts, they consist of the codes of discipline and the clusters of rules, yet one maintains little while transgressing much. As for meditative concentration, it consists of the various levels of *dhyāna* and *samādhi*, yet there is no ground upon which to cultivate them. As for wisdom—
Thus, regarding the wondrous wisdom of the provisional and the ultimate, there is no gate through which one may realize it;

yet if there is even a hair’s breadth of attachment, or if one harbors lingering thoughts for months, or if a single word fails to accord with the truth, one will harbor a grudge for a lifetime—this is easily ignited. This is especially so for those who have merely recently ascended to the level of the precepts.
Once the life-raft has been torn, if one enters the meditation hall and only increases dullness and agitation, success will be difficult to achieve.

Unless one gives rise to deep shame and remorse, severely reproaches oneself, and performs sincere repentance, it will be truly difficult to extinguish transgressions even after passing through kalpas as numerous as dust motes.
Within the method of repentance, one raises the five limbs with diligence to manifest outward respect, and pours forth one’s whole heart.
This clarifies inner reverence. The two elbows, the two knees, and the forehead are called the "five limbs. To "pour forth" means to reveal and cleanse [the heart].
Because one surrenders with sincerity to the Buddha, it is called "surrendering in sincerity. As for "repentance," it is the severing of the continuous flow of the mind.
Because one has practiced evil dharmas in past lives, one now exerts oneself with the five limbs; furthermore, this arises from the mind.
Because greed and anger arose, I now offer my heart with total sincerity. Furthermore, because the tongue uttered evil speech, I now verbally express repentance.
Moreover, because my physical actions (*kāyakarman*) since beginningless time were violent and intense, I now repent with uplifted diligence;

because the mental actions (*manaskarman*) were defiled, I now repent with total sincerity; and because the verbal actions (*vākkarman*) were coarse and wild, I now repent by expressing these words with urgency.
Next, regarding the actual presentation of the repentance: "I" refers to the practitioner speaking for themselves;
"sentient beings" refers to those within the four debts of gratitude, the three realms of existence, and the four modes of birth across the six destinies.

This means that I, together with all sentient beings of the Dharma-realm, from beginningless kalpas until this present life, have constantly given rise to delusions and created karma without ever ceasing. This was not committed by me alone, nor was it...
It was created throughout one's entire life and in a single location, yet it is not the work of a single person; therefore, it says "I and all sentient beings. It is not from a single lifetime;
therefore, it says "from kalpas past until now. It is not in a single place; therefore, it says "immeasurable and boundless.
This is because since beginningless time, sentient beings have, life after life and birth after birth, been mutual relatives, acting as both lords and attendants to one another. Furthermore...
Through mutual assistance, the karmic offenses are fully established. Since the creation of the karma was shared, the repentance must likewise be so.

Therefore, one must universally take all sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm as the object of one’s repentance. Question: Karmic offenses from vast eons ago should have already resulted in their retribution.
Why is it that they remain undestroyed until this very life? If the retribution has already been received, then repentance would not be necessary. If [the retribution has not yet been received]...

If [karma] were not extinguished, then repentance would also be of no benefit. Answer: There are three ways in which sentient beings create karma and receive retribution: first, retribution in the present life; second, retribution in the next life;

and third, retribution in subsequent lives (retribution in the present life is received in this very lifetime; retribution in the next life is received in the immediately following birth; retribution in subsequent lives is received after passing through immeasurable kalpas).
Furthermore, there are two kinds: first, fixed karma; second, unfixed karma. If past karma is destined for retribution in the present life, then it has already been experienced.
As for that which is to be experienced in the next life or in subsequent lives, which is yet to come, how could one not repent with earnest diligence?
Moreover, if it is fixed karma, it cannot be expiated through repentance; if it is unfixed, it is eliminated through repentance.
Extinction. What is meant by "that which is without benefit"? (According to the Small Vehicle, there are fixed and unfixed karmas; according to the Great Vehicle, all are unfixed.

The two phrases concerning "delusion of the fundamentally pure mind" are for repenting the affliction-obstruction (*kleśāvaraṇa*). The four phrases concerning the "defiled three karmas" are for repenting the karma-obstruction (*karmāvaraṇa*).

The two phrases concerning "the retributive karma of enmities formed" are for repenting the retribution-obstruction (*vipākāvaraṇa*). Furthermore, "delusion of the fundamentally pure mind" refers to the fundamental delusions that give free rein to greed.
Hatred and delusion are the branches and leaves of delusion; when speech is confused, it is like clouds covering the moon, so that its radiance does not appear.

When speech is unrestrained, one rears a thief as a son and plunders the family’s treasures for oneself. When the three faculties of body, speech, and mind are associated with afflictions, they are called defilements.
To commit the ten non-virtues and the five heinous crimes is called the stain of transgression. The three karmas are the agents that create these transgressions.

Defilements are what is produced. Once the stains of transgression have been formed, they inevitably summon karmic retribution from enemies. Since every enemy must receive their retribution, it is called an "obstruction of retribution.

Regarding the phrase "immeasurable and boundless," there are briefly five meanings: first, in terms of the mind—a single thought of worldly affliction (*kleśa*) already possesses eighty thousand [forms], let alone those that continue in succession;
second, in terms of objects—what is done in a single location is already immeasurable in itself; how much more so...
How much more so for the ten directions. Third, regarding the nature of the act: if even a single karma were completed, the resulting transgression would be boundless;
how much more so for all karmas? Fourth, regarding time: what one has done in a single lifetime should already be immeasurable, how much more so over kalpas of vast duration?

Fifth, regarding persons: what one individual has done is already itself boundless, how much more so for all sentient beings? Therefore, if karma had form, it would be difficult for empty space to contain it.
It is indeed so. There are three types of karmic enmity. As it is said: "When a person dies, they become a sheep; when a sheep dies, they become a person.
Thus, through death after death and birth after birth, they devour one another in turn. This is called the enmity of killing. "You owe me my life, and I shall repay you with my debt";
for hundreds of thousands of kalpas, one remains constantly within birth and death. This is called the enmity of theft. "You love my mind, and I cherish your form. For... [text continues]

For hundreds of thousands of kalpas, one remains constantly in bondage; this is called the grievance of lust (*kāma-vaira*). [Question: Since there is no resentment between the two parties in lust, why is it also called a "grievance"? [Answer:

The two karmas of killing and stealing are called the "grievance of anger" (*krodha-vaira*), while lust is called the "grievance of joy" (*rati-vaira*). Both anger and joy are grievances, and there is nothing that is not karma. It is precisely because of this that sentient beings, through their perversion, mistake enemies for kin. May all of these be completely extinguished.
This refers to the simultaneous extinction of the three obstacles. This concludes the second section: Repentance of the Three Obstacles. △ Third, the Making of Vows, which has three parts:
first, the general vow; second, the specific vows; third, the summary conclusion. Now, the first: the general vow.

From this day forth, I establish profound vows: I vow to remain far removed from unwholesome dharmas and never again commit them; I vow to diligently cultivate the Noble Path without ever falling back or succumbing to indolence;
I vow to attain perfect enlightenment; and I vow to deliver all sentient beings.
These are the four great vows (*mahāpraṇidhāna*). If one practices without vows, there will be regression and loss;

therefore, by using these four dharmas to restrain one's own mind, one will not give rise to indolence. These four great vows are generated based on the non-arising Four Noble Truths (*anabhisaṃskṛta-catur-āryasatya*) of the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya*);
they are called "profound vows. If a vow does not rely upon the Truths, it is called "madness."
Vow. If it were not non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*), it would not be called profound.
What is meant by "non-action" is that the four [truths] are all inherently complete and involve no deliberate construction. Master Tiantai said:

"Because of delusion regarding the principle, nirvāṇa is saṃsāra and is termed the Truth of Suffering; bodhi is affliction and is termed the Truth of Origination. Because of awakening to the principle..."
Death is itself *nirvāṇa*; this is called the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*). Afflictions (*kleśa*) are themselves awakening (*bodhi*);
this is called the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*). I shall now briefly explain this. Birth-and-death and afflictions are the cause and effect of sentient beings;

awakening and *nirvāṇa* are the cause and effect of the Buddhas. However, both sentient beings and Buddhas exist only as names; birth-and-death, afflictions, awakening, and *nirvāṇa* are likewise [mere names].
These exist only as names. When investigated to the ultimate limit, they are nothing but the one mind.
Because from beginningless time we have been deluded regarding this one mind, we have taken enlightenment and nirvana entirely to be afflictions and birth-and-death.
Therefore, on this day, by awakening to this one mind, we take those very afflictions and birth-and-death to be enlightenment and nirvana. Although there are two names, their essence—

Thus, there is no duality. It is like water forming ice, and ice returning to water; this is precisely the "unconditioned Four Noble Truths. [Question: If it is true that sentient beings and Buddhas exist merely as names, then birth-and-death and afflictions are defiled dharmas, while bodhi and nirvana are pure dharmas. Their ascent and descent are vastly different, and their excellence and inferiority are as distinct as heaven and abyss. How can you say that these too exist merely as names? [Answer: If we discuss this from the perspective of phenomena (*dharma*), it is indeed as you have said. However, if we examine it according to principle (*li*), each and every one of them lacks any real substance. To use an analogy: it is like actors in a pear orchard (*li-yuan*) who dress up as poor beggars; though they physically go about begging for food, their minds harbor expectations [of wealth and status]. In the same way, although the names of birth-and-death and nirvana are established, when examined by principle, they are ultimately non-dual. Therefore, it is said that all dharmas are empty and without self-nature. This is what is meant by the "unconditioned Four Noble Truths. Furthermore, because the Four Noble Truths are unconditioned, they are not subject to arising or ceasing, nor do they involve the activity of conditioned existence. They are simply the ultimate reality of the nature of dharmas. Thus, it is said that the Four Noble Truths are unconditioned. Because they are unconditioned, they transcend the realm of birth-and-death and are identical with the Dharma-realm. Because they are identical with the Dharma-realm, they are the very essence of the Buddha. Because they are the essence of the Buddha, they are the Tathāgata. Because they are the Tathāgata, they are the Great Nirvana. Because they are Great Nirvana, they are the Great Vehicle. Because they are the Great Vehicle, they are the Mahāyāna. Because they are the Mahāyāna, they are the One Vehicle. Because they are the One Vehicle, they are the Buddha Vehicle. Because they are the Buddha Vehicle, they are the Vehicle of the Tathāgata. Because they are the Vehicle of Wisdom, they are the Vehicle of Liberation. Because they are the Vehicle of Liberation, they are the Vehicle of Emptiness. Because they are the Vehicle of Emptiness, they are the Vehicle of Non-arising. Because they are the Vehicle of Non-arising, they are the Vehicle of Non-extinction. Because they are the Vehicle of Non-extinction, they are the Vehicle of Non-duality. Because they are the Vehicle of Non-duality, they are the Vehicle of Non-distinction. Because they are the Vehicle of Non-distinction, they are the Vehicle of Equality. Because they are the Vehicle of Equality, they are the Vehicle of Sameness. Because they are the Vehicle of Sameness, they are the Vehicle of Purity. Because they are the Vehicle of Purity, they are the Vehicle of Tranquility. Because they are the Vehicle of Tranquility, they are the Vehicle of Stillness. Because they are the Vehicle of Stillness, they are the Vehicle of Non-action. Because they are the Vehicle of Non-action, they are the Vehicle of Non-attainment. Because they are the Vehicle of Non-attainment, they are the Vehicle of Non-abiding. Because they are the Vehicle of Non-abiding, they are the Vehicle of Non-return. Because they are the Vehicle of Non-return, they are the Vehicle of Non-departure. Because they are the Vehicle of Non-departure, they are the Vehicle of Non-existence. Because they are the Vehicle of Non-existence, they are the Vehicle of Non-non-existence. Because they are the Vehicle of Non-non-existence, they are the Vehicle of Non-discrimination. Because they are the Vehicle of Non-discrimination, they are the Vehicle of Non-conceptualization. Because they are the Vehicle of Non-conceptualization, they are the Vehicle of Non-manifestation. Because they are the Vehicle of Non-manifestation, they are the Vehicle of Non-appearance. Because they are the Vehicle of Non-appearance, they are the Vehicle of Non-characteristics. Because they are the Vehicle of Non-characteristics, they are the Vehicle of Non-form.
